summaries.headline: NYC Reading Scores Drop Amid Curriculum Overhaul
summaries.summary: New York City reading proficiency fell 6 percentage points across grades 3-8 last school year, nearly wiping out the prior year's gains, with third graders posting a nearly 14-point decline and fifth graders dropping 13 points. The slide comes in the fourth year of a citywide mandate requiring elementary schools to adopt science-of-reading curriculums, and officials note the state test results contradict the city's own periodic assessments, which showed improvement. Chancellor Kamar Samuels has ordered an analysis of the discrepancy, while the teachers union blames the district for layering on additional programs and consultants instead of sticking to a focused instructional plan.

summaries.headline: Colorado District Strips Bible Content From Reading Curriculum
summaries.summary: The Montezuma-Cortez district in southwestern Colorado will remove or modify biblically infused material from its new elementary reading curriculum after facing scrutiny over the Texas-developed Bluebonnet program. Superintendent Eddie Ramirez outlined the changes in an open letter to parents and staff, stating schools "will not use the curriculum as a vehicle for religious instruction," and the 2,200-student district scheduled a special board meeting to formally adopt the curriculum after administrators had rolled it out in July without a board vote. The episode traces back to the district's adoption of Houston Superintendent Mike Miles' New Education System model, underscoring how borrowing instructional frameworks across state lines can import content misaligned with local academic standards and community expectations.

summaries.headline: First Evaluation of Pay-for-Results Vendor Contracts Emerges
summaries.summary: A growing number of districts are adopting outcomes-based contracting, a purchasing model that ties vendor payment to whether tutoring and ed-tech programs actually move student achievement, with Michigan now requiring it for a $50 million virtual tutoring fund and more than 20 other states experimenting with the approach. WestEd's first independent evaluation of eight early-adopter districts across California, Florida, Mississippi and Texas found three interventions produced measurable academic gains, but researchers could only rigorously analyze 4 of 10 programs studied, and one tutoring program ran for just two months instead of a full school year, too short to expect results. The findings suggest outcomes-based contracts can work, but only when programs are actually implemented as designed and districts have the capacity to track and measure results — a caveat that complicates the push to scale this model quickly.

summaries.headline: School Funding Follows a Surprising U-Shaped Pattern
summaries.summary: A Brookings Institution analysis challenges the conventional wisdom that property taxes drive deep funding gaps between rich and poor school systems, finding instead that both high- and low-poverty districts tend to outspend those in the middle. The U-shaped pattern holds even after adjusting for regional differences in personnel costs, and separate research shows that while poor children see slightly more spent on their formal education, they face far larger gaps in resources supporting their well-being outside school. Researchers still agree high-poverty districts need more funding to serve their students effectively, suggesting the real equity problem lies less in the mechanics of school finance and more in what happens beyond the schoolhouse door.

summaries.headline: UFT Threatens to Pull Support for NYC Reads
summaries.summary: UFT President Michael Mulgrew is threatening to withdraw the teachers union's backing of NYC Reads, the citywide literacy curriculum mandate, just as Mayor Zohran Mamdani pushes to expand it and weeks after reading scores dropped across the district. Mulgrew still supports the core shift to common reading curriculums but says the city has piled on excessive requirements, including at least three student assessments per year and mandatory intervention programs that don't align with schools' chosen curriculums, while also walking back earlier promises to let teachers implement changes at their own pace. The standoff marks another rift between City Hall and the union, following Mamdani's recent retreats on paraprofessional pay raises and class-size reduction timelines, and signals that the mayor's literacy agenda could face resistance just as it moves toward expansion rather than consolidation.

summaries.headline: School Funding Follows a U-Shaped Curve
summaries.summary: A new Brookings Institution analysis finds that school funding in the U.S. doesn't follow the pattern many assume, with high-poverty and low-poverty school systems both tending to outspend those in the middle. The finding challenges the conventional narrative that funding scales neatly with poverty levels, pointing instead to a more complicated distribution shaped by local, state, and federal funding formulas. For district leaders advocating for equitable resources, the data complicates simple appeals based on poverty alone and suggests the funding conversation needs a more nuanced framework.

summaries.headline: Parents, Educators Want More Data Literacy Instruction
summaries.summary: A new survey from Mathematica finds that parents and educators view data literacy as a critical skill in the age of artificial intelligence, yet believe schools aren't providing enough opportunities for students to develop it. Data literacy—the ability to question, evaluate, interpret, and communicate information—is increasingly seen as foundational rather than a niche technical skill, particularly as AI tools become embedded in daily academic and professional life. The gap between perceived importance and actual instructional access suggests districts may need to rethink where data and AI literacy fit in curriculum planning, not as electives but as core competencies.

summaries.headline: Great Minds Expands Into Foundational Literacy Market
summaries.summary: Great Minds PBC launched Arts & Letters: Reading Foundations, a K-5 early reading and screening product built to align with its existing Arts & Letters K-8 core ELA curriculum. The product grew out of a March partnership with Magpie Literacy, a K-2 literacy platform, and marks the second new market entry for the company in six months following its move into high school ELA. District leaders evaluating curriculum coherence across foundational skills and core ELA now have another vertically aligned option from a major publisher expanding well beyond its original math roots.

summaries.headline: CPS Can't Fully Reverse Teacher Layoffs
summaries.summary: Chicago's Board of Education voted 11-7 to reverse hundreds of summer layoffs, but district officials say the money won't stretch far enough to bring everyone back. The revised budget banks on $150 million in additional state funding, with $100 million earmarked for reinstatements, yet CPS hasn't disclosed how many of the laid-off teachers and support staff will actually return before the Aug. 24 start date. Principals won't have to reopen finalized budgets — instead, the district will centrally hire back "selected positions" based on survey responses, leaving thousands of educators waiting to learn their fate just weeks before students arrive.

summaries.headline: Judge Voids Board's "Public Christian School" Deal
summaries.summary: A Colorado district court judge ruled that the Pueblo County School District 70 board violated the state's open meetings law by obscuring the religious nature of Riverstone Academy, a "public Christian school" the board approved in June 2025 before it closed permanently this past May. The ruling invalidates that approval agreement along with a February appointment to fill a vacant board seat, potentially opening the door for the state to recover roughly $300,000 in public funding already disbursed to the school, and requires the board to cover the plaintiffs' attorney fees. Board members have authorized an immediate appeal if forced to redo the vacancy vote, signaling that questions about transparency, religious instruction, and public school funding in Pueblo 70 are far from settled.

summaries.headline: Denver Voters to Decide on $44M School Tax
summaries.summary: Denver voters will weigh a $44 million property tax increase in November to fund raises and expanded services for Denver Public Schools, with the school board voting unanimously to place the measure on the ballot. Of the total, $25.8 million would go toward a flat $1,750 raise for every full-time employee, while the remainder would fund career and technical education programming, mental health supports, and special education services; the increase would cost the owner of a median-priced Denver home about $72 a year. The measure comes as DPS, the state's largest district with 89,000 students, grapples with declining enrollment, rising health insurance and utility costs, and growing special education needs — a combination squeezing budgets in per-pupil funded states well beyond Denver.

summaries.headline: Missouri's Charter Funding Fix Falls Short
summaries.summary: Missouri lawmakers passed HB 1552 in 2022 aiming to close the nation's largest charter school funding gap, a shortfall that once stood at $3,638 per student. By 2024-25, the law had boosted total state and local revenues for the state's charter schools—all based in Kansas City and St. Louis—by nearly $4,000 per pupil, offsetting most of the roughly 25 percent funding gap that existed before the law took effect. A Fordham Institute study now examines what that infusion actually bought in terms of spending and achievement, offering other states a real-world test of whether narrowing the gap on paper translates into narrowing outcomes in practice.

summaries.headline: A Roadmap for Navigating California's School Budget Fight
summaries.summary: The California Budget & Policy Center has released a guide breaking down how the state's budget process shapes funding for TK-12 education, walking advocates through the terminology, deadlines, and roles the governor and Legislature play in deciding how dollars flow to schools. The state budget provides most of the funding for California's 5.7 million public school students, and the guide details three key deadlines and specific windows where advocacy input carries the most weight before decisions are finalized. For district leaders and education advocates unfamiliar with Sacramento's budget calendar, the guide offers a practical entry point into a process that determines resources long before any dollar reaches a classroom.

summaries.headline: Colorado District Pulls Texas Reading Curriculum Over Errors
summaries.summary: The Montezuma-Cortez school board voted 4-3 to reject Bluebonnet, a Texas-developed reading curriculum, just three days into the school year, forcing elementary staff to scramble for replacement lessons. Board Vice President Laura DeWitt flagged what she called "robot errors" likely generated by AI, including a map placing Houston next to the Florida panhandle instead of Texas — mistakes layered on top of thousands of errors Texas is already spending $8 million to correct. The episode raises broader questions for districts eyeing out-of-state curriculum products: adoption speed and vendor track record matter as much as content alignment when materials cross state lines.

summaries.headline: NYC Reading Scores Slip During Curriculum Overhaul
summaries.summary: New York City's latest reading scores show a decline as the district works through a major overhaul of its literacy instruction, shifting schools away from balanced literacy toward phonics-based, "science of reading" approaches. The dip comes during a multiyear transition that has required retraining thousands of teachers and replacing long-used curricula across hundreds of schools, the kind of disruption researchers often flag as a predictable cost of large-scale instructional change. District leaders elsewhere weighing similar reading reforms will be watching whether NYC's numbers rebound in later cohorts or whether the transition itself needs recalibration.

summaries.headline: New Report Links Absenteeism to Academic Decline
summaries.summary: A new report examines the connection between chronic absenteeism and slower academic progress in K-12 students, adding to a growing body of research on attendance as a core instructional concern. The underlying article did not include the report's specific data points or methodology, limiting the ability to detail exact figures or affected grade bands. For district leaders already tracking post-pandemic attendance recovery, the findings reinforce that consistent presence in the classroom remains a prerequisite for academic gains, not a separate policy issue to address after the fact.

summaries.headline: K-12 Payrolls Shrink for First Time Since COVID
summaries.summary: Public schools shed 50,000 workers from June to July, according to the latest Bureau of Labor Statistics report, with May's figures also revised down by 47,000. Stripping out seasonal adjustments, K-12 employment now sits about 29,000 below where it stood a year ago, marking the first year-over-year decline since pandemic-era school closures forced layoffs of bus drivers, cafeteria staff, and other support personnel. The numbers remain preliminary and subject to revision, but they break a five-year streak of steady payroll growth that district leaders have come to expect.

summaries.headline: Strategic Education Expands Startup Pilot Network
summaries.summary: Strategic Education Inc. has opened applications for the second cohort of Signal Labs, a program that pairs growth-stage edtech and workforce-tech startups with its network of institutions, including Strayer University, Capella University, and Torrens University, for unpaid product pilots. Two new venture partners, Rethink Capital Partners and New Markets Venture Partners, join returning backer LearnLaunch Fund + Accelerator, whose broader portfolio spans more than 50 education and workforce companies; the first cohort, launched in June 2026, already paired an AI job-search platform and a project-based work experience provider with career services teams across the network. For K-12 leaders tracking the pipeline between secondary schools and workforce-aligned higher ed, the model offers a preview of how postsecondary institutions are vetting new tools before scaling them — a structured, data-sharing approach that could inform how districts evaluate edtech

summaries.headline: Louisiana District Adds Targeted Dyslexia Instruction
summaries.summary: Caldwell Parish School District will launch a dyslexia training program from the Masonic Learning Center of Louisiana no later than Labor Day, aimed at students ages 8 to 17. Superintendent Nikki McCann framed the initiative as a way to close gaps left by standard reading instruction for students who continue to struggle despite existing supports, while program coordinator Michelle Dempsey said the goal is equipping identified students with strategies to manage dyslexia's daily academic effects. The move reflects a broader pattern of districts turning to specialized, targeted interventions rather than relying solely on general reading curricula to serve students with diagnosed learning differences.

summaries.headline: Louisiana Task Force to Rework School Funding Formula
summaries.summary: Louisiana lawmakers launched a Minimum Foundation Program Formula Task Force after educators packed a capitol committee room to press for stable funding of teacher and support staff bonuses. The $2,000 teacher and $1,000 support staff bonuses, paid by the state for three years, shifted to local districts after voters rejected a constitutional amendment last spring and Governor Landry ordered districts to cover the costs, pushing some — including East Feliciana Parish — to draw from reserve funds they may not have. The task force will spend until January examining district spending patterns and possible per-pupil formula adjustments, leaving districts to absorb bonus costs in the meantime even as Louisiana teacher pay continues to lag neighboring states.

synthesis.topic_title: 50-State Tracker: School Funding Formulas Face a Trust Problem
synthesis.whats_happening: States are grappling with two distinct funding challenges this cycle: whether formulas distribute money fairly, and whether anyone outside the state capitol can actually explain how those formulas work. Wyoming and Indiana are both turning to public-facing tools to demystify funding mechanics, while Tennessee voters face school funding as one line item in a crowded November ballot. Ohio, meanwhile, shows how categorical funding streams continue to operate as a parallel track to core formula debates.

Advocacy pressure for needs-based, equity-driven distribution is resurfacing in at least one state, suggesting formula fairness remains an unresolved post-pandemic tension. Ballot bundling in Tennessee signals that school funding is increasingly litigated through general fiscal referenda rather than standalone education votes.

Anyone wanting to better understand Indiana public school finances can now learn the basics through a 6-minute animated video, two statewide education organizations announced Thursday.

The Indiana Association of School Business Officials and Indiana School Public Relations Association partnered to produce the video to help make the complex topic easier for families, taxpayers and community members to understand, a news release said.

The video describes public school districts’ main revenue sources – state dollars, local property taxes and federal grants – and how districts can spend and manage their funding.

Understanding school finance shouldn’t require special expertise, said Krista Stockman, the president of the public relations group. The association represents more than 200 members from more than 100 districts.

“Our members regularly hear questions from parents, staff members and community members about where school funding comes from and how those dollars are used,” Stockman, who is also the Fort Wayne Community Schools communication director, said in a statement.

“We wanted to create something districts could share that provides a clear, accessible starting point for those conversations.”

Greater understanding of education funding can help communities have more informed conversations about their schools, said Scott Bowling, executive director of the business officials association.

The group supports those responsible for the financial and operational management of Indiana’s public schools.

“School business officials have a responsibility not only to manage public resources carefully, but also to help stakeholders understand how those resources support students,” Bowling said in a statement.

“This video provides districts with another tool to communicate about school funding clearly and transparently.”

The associations are encouraging districts statewide to share the video, suggesting it can be used during school board meetings, among other places.

School boards will hold their annual public budgets hearings this fall. Information about dates and times will be posted to the Indiana Gateway at [budgetnotices.in.gov](https://budgetnotices.in.gov/).

The state budget calendar indicates Nov. 2 is the deadline for all taxing units to adopt next year’s budgets, tax rates and tax levies.

COLUMBUS, Ohio – The city of Niles and Howland Township are among the communities that will share in Ohio’s $8.8 million investment in projects that make it safer and easier for students to walk or bike to school.

Niles was awarded $500,000 to upgrade and install new pedestrian features to the main sidewalk, crosswalks and traffic signals in the area of Niles Middle School.

Howland will receive $77,000 to construct a sidewalk along the east side of Niles Cortland Road NE to improve pedestrian safety and access for school-age children. The project will include 5,931 feet of sidewalk between High Street and Carriage Hill, addressing the most significant gap in the corridor.

The funding is part of the Ohio Department of Transportation’s [Safe Routes to School](https://links-2.govdelivery.com/CL0/https:%2F%2Fwww.transportation.ohio.gov%2Fbusiness%2Ffunding%2Fsafe-routes-to-school/1/0101019ffbb23826-a609468f-7d8e-4741-bd29-07074f09f5ef-000000/dv64_BHkcxtc94HcyhQGQJC6U4mGQFtrzPnokyoSgxg=452) program, which helps communities build and improve infrastructure such as sidewalks, crosswalks, bike lanes and traffic-calming features.

“Investing in our children’s safety, health and well-being is one of the most important things we can do for Ohio’s future,” Gov. Mike DeWine said. “These Safe Routes to School grants empower local communities and give families peace of mind that their student can safely walk or bike to school every single day.”

Since its inception in 2005, the program has awarded nearly $100 million to schools, municipalities, health districts, park districts and nonprofit organizations working to improve student safety and promote active transportation.

“Every child deserves a safe, accessible path to school, whether they’re walking, riding a bike or using a scooter,” said Pamela Boratyn, ODOT director. “By investing in pedestrian and bike infrastructure, we are creating healthier, more connected communities across all of Ohio.”

NASHVILLE — Senate Democratic Leader Sen. Raumesh Akbari, D-Memphis, released the following statement Friday after Tennessee’s primary elections set the field for November:

“Tennesseans are working hard, but too many families feel like their paychecks don’t stretch as far as they used to. Groceries, child care, health care, electricity and housing all cost more. This November, voters deserve a real conversation about what we can do to make life more affordable.

“Democrats have a plan. Repeal the grocery tax and put more than $800 million back into Tennesseans’ pockets by closing corporate tax loopholes. Make pre-K universal for 4-year-olds so children get a stronger start and parents have more options to work. Bring $1.4 billion in federal health care funding home every year to help keep hospitals open and expand coverage. Invest in public schools instead of pouring a billion dollars into private school vouchers. And pass Pot for Potholes to rebuild roads and bridges in communities across Tennessee.

“These aren’t slogans or promises we came up with for election season. They’re real bills we’ve introduced, fought for and put before the legislature — with real sponsors and real ways to pay for them. We’ve been ready to work with anyone willing to move good ideas forward.

“For too long, too many of these proposals haven’t even been given a real chance. Meanwhile, families are still paying the grocery tax, hospitals are struggling, child care is out of reach for too many parents, and communities are waiting on basic infrastructure improvements.

“That’s the choice this November. We can keep doing what we’ve been doing, or we can choose a government that works as hard as the people it represents. Democrats are ready to lower costs, strengthen public schools, expand access to health care and make sure that whether you live in Memphis, Mountain City or anywhere in between, you have a fair shot at building a good life right here in Tennessee.”

# Staffordshire calls for fairer school funding to help children and young people

10 August 2026


![Janet Higgins in a school](https://www.staffordshire.gov.uk/sites/default/files/styles/large_3_2_768x512/public/2026-07/Janet%20Higgins%20school_cropped_0.jpg?itok=cEq67odj)

**Staffordshire County Council is calling on the Government to review how schools and special educational needs funding is allocated.**

Councillor Janet Higgins, Staffordshire County Council's Cabinet Member for Education and SEND, [has written to Lucy Powell MP, Secretary of State for Education](https://www.staffordshire.gov.uk/sites/default/files/2026-08/Letter%20Re%20Fair%20Funding%20for%20Staffordshire.pdf), asking the Government to tackle long-standing inequalities in the way funding is shared out.

The council says Staffordshire receives some of the lowest levels of funding in England for schools and for support for children and young people with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND).

Almost 11,100 children and young people in Staffordshire currently have Education, Health and Care Plans (EHCPs), and demand for support continues to rise each year.

The council is working to improve services, help more children learn in mainstream schools where appropriate, and create more local specialist places. However, funding has not kept up with growing need.

The council's analysis shows Staffordshire gets less funding per pupil than the national average and many similar councils. If Staffordshire received funding in line with national averages, schools in the county could get tens of millions of pounds more each year.

The council says this funding gap is putting pressure on the whole education system. More children need SEND support, specialist placements are becoming more expensive, and transport costs are rising.

Janet Higgins said:

> "Every child in Staffordshire deserves the best possible start in life and the support they need to achieve their full potential.
>
> "Our schools, teachers and support staff do a fantastic job, but they are being asked to do more and more with less funding than many other areas of the country receive.
>
> "The number of children and young people needing SEND support continues to grow. We as a council are investing in local provision and working hard to improve services, however the current funding system simply is not fair to Staffordshire.
>
> “As a large rural county, we also face additional costs, particularly home to school and SEND transport, that are not fully recognised. We need a funding system that reflects real need and gives every child the same opportunities, regardless of where they live.
>
> “I am asking the Government to look again at how funding is allocated and work with councils like Staffordshire to create a fairer system that supports children, families and schools both now and in the future."

In the letter, the council asks the Government to:

- Review the National Funding Formula to make it fairer.
- Increase school and High Needs funding for councils that currently receive less.
- Recognise the extra costs faced by large rural counties, including transport for children and young people with SEND.
- Support earlier help and more inclusive mainstream education.
- Improve how funding for education, SEND, post-16 education and employment is joined up.

The council says fair funding is important for schools and for Staffordshire's future. It would help improve skills, support the workforce of the future and give children and young people better opportunities.
